claims.statement: In a nationally representative US survey of 202,248 adults aged 25 or older (113,752 women and 88,496 men, interviewed in 1997 to 2004 and followed through death records for about 7 years on average, to the end of 2006), people who currently smoked cigarettes compared with people who had smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in their lives died at about three times the rate at ages 25 to 79 (adjusted hazard ratio 3.0 in women, 99% CI 2.7 to 3.3; 2.8 in men, 2.4 to 3.1). The ratio was largest for lung cancer (17.8 in women, 14.6 in men) and respiratory disease (8.5 and 9.0), about 3 for ischemic heart disease (3.5 and 3.2) and for stroke in women (3.2), and 1.7 for stroke in men, with an interval from 1.0 to 2.8. The authors estimate that about 6 in 10 of the deaths among people who currently smoked at these ages (62% in women, 60% in men) would have been avoided if their death rates from disease had matched those of people who never smoked. Scaled to US death rates for 2004, they estimate that 38 in 100 women and 26 in 100 men who currently smoked would survive from age 25 to 80, against 70 in 100 women and 61 in 100 men who never smoked, a difference of about 11 and 12 years of life. Compared with people who continued to smoke, people who had stopped gained about 10, 9, 6 and 4 years of life when they stopped at 25 to 34, 35 to 44, 45 to 54 and 55 to 64 years of age (read from survival curves). Those who stopped at 35 to 44 (median 39) still had 1.2 times the death rate of people who never smoked, against 3.0 for people who continued: the authors read this as an excess cut by about 90% and call the remaining excess substantial (about 1 in 6 of such people who died before 80 would not have died at the rate of people who never smoked). These are averages for groups, not what any one person would gain, and they concern cigarette smoking only. Smoking was recorded once, at the interview, so people who stopped afterwards stay in the smoking group; the amount smoked, other tobacco products, vapes and pouches were not examined; adjustment covered age, education, alcohol and body-mass index but not diet, physical activity or income; and the paper does not show the authors' checks of what adjustment, national scaling and leaving out the first two years of follow-up changed. The US Surgeon General's 2014 report, as summarized in its listed conclusions, judges the evidence sufficient to infer that cigarette smoking increases the risk of death from any cause in men and women and that it is the dominant cause of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and states that cigarette smoking is causally linked to disease in nearly all organs; those listed conclusions give no change in the risk of death or of the main diseases after stopping, apart from a better prognosis for people with cancer and, graded suggestive but not sufficient, a lower risk of advanced age-related macular degeneration. The cohort study was funded by the US National Institutes of Health (Fogarty International Center), the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Gates Foundation's Disease Control Priorities Project; no tobacco-industry funding is printed. Certainty: moderate. Status: single study.
claims.population: US adults aged 25 or older in the National Health Interview Survey, interviewed 1997 to 2004 (113,752 women and 88,496 men analysed; 15,715 deaths to the end of 2006; mean follow-up about 7 years)
claims.exposure: Currently smoking cigarettes at the interview (23,839 women and 23,348 men), counting people who stopped within 5 years before death as still smoking; stopping at 25 to 34, 35 to 44, 45 to 54 or 55 to 64 years of age (medians 29, 39, 49 and 59)
claims.comparator: Having smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in a lifetime (67,524 women and 39,289 men); for stopping, people who continued to smoke
claims.outcome: Death from any cause and from lung cancer, ischemic heart disease, stroke, respiratory disease and other causes at ages 25 to 79; modelled probability of surviving from age 25 to 80; years of life gained by stopping
claims.magnitude: Adjusted hazard ratios (99% CI), current smoking against never smoking, ages 25 to 79, women / men: all causes 3.0 (2.7 to 3.3) / 2.8 (2.4 to 3.1); lung cancer 17.8 (11.4 to 27.8) / 14.6 (9.1 to 23.4); ischemic heart disease 3.5 (2.7 to 4.6) / 3.2 (2.5 to 4.1); stroke 3.2 (2.2 to 4.7) / 1.7 (1.0 to 2.8); respiratory disease 8.5 (6.1 to 11.8) / 9.0 (5.6 to 14.4); all cancers 3.2 (2.6 to 3.9) / 3.8 (3.1 to 4.8). Deaths from any cause in the never-smoked and current groups: 2,190 and 1,579 in women, 1,283 and 2,030 in men; all-cause ratios 3.1 and 2.8 after excluding people who stopped within 5 years before death and people with earlier heart disease, stroke or cancer. Share of deaths among people who currently smoked that would have been avoided at never-smoked disease death rates: 62% (59 to 65) in women and 60% (55 to 63) in men (accidents and injuries, about 7% of the excess, not counted). Probability of surviving from 25 to 80, scaled to 2004 US death rates, never smoked against currently smoking: women 70% (99% CI 64 to 76) against 38% (30 to 45); men 61% (55 to 67) against 26% (18 to 33); gaps of 32 and 35 percentage points (editors' subtraction) and about 11 and 12 years. Stopping against continuing to smoke: about 10, 9, 6 and 4 years of life gained at 25 to 34, 35 to 44, 45 to 54 and 55 to 64 (no intervals given in the text); hazard ratio 1.2 for those who stopped at 35 to 44 against people who never smoked, 3.0 for those who continued (excess of 0.2 against 2.0, about 90% less, editors' arithmetic); excess cut by about two thirds for stopping at 45 to 54.
claims.reasoning: Observational (a national survey linked to death records), so it starts low. Upgraded one level for a large effect: the all-cause ratio is about 3 (lower limit 2.4) and the lung cancer ratios are 15 to 18, they stay at 3.1 and 2.8 in the printed sensitivity analysis, and the biases that remain (smoking measured once, which pushes toward 1; four adjustment variables; cause-of-death misclassification, which does not touch the all-cause ratios) are not expected to produce a ratio of this size. Not downgraded for risk of bias (ROBINS-E: some concerns, none likely to account for a threefold ratio); read strictly, without the upgrade, the rating would be low. The rating applies to the all-cause, lung cancer, respiratory and heart disease ratios and to the survival figures; the stroke ratio in men (1.7, interval 1.0 to 2.8), the years of life gained by stopping (read from survival curves, with no intervals given in the text; the all-cause ratios for people who had stopped are in a supplementary table that was not opened) and the 90% figure (measured for one age group) are less certain, taken alone they would be rated low, and the statement words them so. The Surgeon General's 2014 conclusions are second-hand (a narrative review with no stated search) and are used for context only. Status single study because only the survey cohort was read: Jha et al. describe four other prospective studies as giving similar ratios, and reading them could move the status to replicated. The survey is run by a US federal agency and the analysis was funded by public bodies and a charitable foundation; no industry funding is printed (the disclosure forms were not opened).

current_lines.q: How much does smoking shorten life?
current_lines.short: About 11 to 12 years on average, a big US study estimates. Of 100 women who smoked, 38 would reach 80, against 70 who never smoked.
current_lines.but: These are averages for groups in one US study, not a forecast for any one person. It looked at cigarettes only.
how: About 202,000 US adults aged 25 or older were interviewed in 1997 to 2004 and followed through death records for about 7 years. At ages 25 to 79, people who smoked died at about 3 times the rate of people who never smoked (under 100 cigarettes in their lives).

The gap was biggest for lung cancer, at about 15 to 18 times the rate, and other lung and breathing diseases, about 8 to 9 times. For heart disease it was about 3 times. The authors estimate that about 6 in 10 deaths among people who smoked at these ages wouldn't have happened at the disease death rates of people who never smoked.

Scaled to US death rates in 2004, 38 in 100 women and 26 in 100 men who smoked would live from 25 to 80, against 70 and 61 in 100 who never smoked. A 2014 US Surgeon General's report judges that smoking raises the risk of dying and causes disease in nearly every organ.

Compared with people who kept smoking, people who had stopped gained roughly 10 years if they stopped at 25 to 34, 9 at 35 to 44, 6 at 45 to 54 and 4 at 55 to 64. Those who stopped around 40 still died at 1.2 times the rate of people who never smoked, against 3 times for those who kept on.
current_lines.rate: One large nationwide study, linked to death records. It didn't account for diet, exercise or income, but those are unlikely to explain a death rate three times as high. The figures on stopping are rougher.

myth_or_fact_items.statement: Quitting smoking between 55 and 64 is too late to make any difference.
myth_or_fact_items.why: In a big US study, people who stopped at 55 to 64 gained roughly 4 years compared with people who kept smoking. That's a group average.

myth_or_fact_items.statement: Quitting smoking around 40 wipes out all the extra risk of dying early.
myth_or_fact_items.why: In a big US study, people who stopped around 40 still died at 1.2 times the rate of people who never smoked, against 3 times for those who kept smoking.

lines_he_saw_on_13_november.q: How much does smoking shorten life?
lines_he_saw_on_13_november.short: On average, people who smoke cigarettes die 11 to 12 years sooner than people who never smoked.
lines_he_saw_on_13_november.but: One large US study. These are averages for groups, not a forecast for one person.
how: About 200,000 US adults were followed for about 7 years. People who smoked died at about 3 times the rate of people who never smoked.
Of 100 women who smoke, about 38 would live to 80, against 70 of 100 who never smoked. For men: 26 against 61.
Stopping gave years back: about 10 years for people who stopped at 25 to 34, and about 4 for people who stopped at 55 to 64.
A 2014 US Surgeon General's report also judges that smoking causes disease in nearly every part of the body.

claims.statement: As described in the US Surgeon General's 2014 report (a narrative review with no stated search method; its figures are second-hand here), the burden of death and disease from tobacco in the United States is overwhelmingly caused by cigarettes and other combusted tobacco products; the report states this as a conclusion about products and does not divide the harm between nicotine and the other substances in smoke. For nicotine on its own, compared with burning tobacco and with no tobacco use, its chapter on nicotine grades six conclusions. Sufficient to infer a causal relationship: nicotine is acutely toxic at high enough doses (drawn from animal studies, medicine trials and poisoning reports, with no systematic dose-response assessment); nicotine activates biological pathways through which smoking raises the risk of disease (experimental research); nicotine exposure in the fetus has lasting adverse effects on brain development (the chapter's support is brief and experimental, with a pointer to a later chapter that was not read; it describes no human study that separates nicotine from the rest of the smoke); and nicotine adversely affects maternal and fetal health in pregnancy, contributing to preterm delivery and stillbirth (inferred from studies of smokeless tobacco in Sweden and India, trials of nicotine replacement in pregnancy and experiments; for example Swedish snus and small-for-gestational-age term births, adjusted odds ratio 1.21, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.43, smaller than for smoking (the report's printed figure for smoking is a misprint and is not quoted), and, in a trial of 250 pregnant women, higher birth weight in the nicotine-patch group than in the placebo group, 186 g, 95% CI 35 to 336, with no difference in quit rates, possibly because of less smoking; the chapter reads the studies together as supporting a modest role for nicotine in fetal growth restriction). Outside its graded conclusions, the chapter's summary says animal studies, including in primates, consistently show that nicotine may be the primary mediator of many of the adverse effects of maternal smoking on fetal lung development. Suggestive but not sufficient: nicotine exposure in adolescence may have lasting adverse effects on brain development (smoking in adolescence is linked to lasting cognitive and behavioural problems, but confounding makes cause hard to establish). Inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship: nicotine and cancer (genotoxicity data are mixed; animal studies mostly do not show nicotine alone to cause tumours; the one human follow-up of people who used nicotine replacement long term, a short one, had 75 lung cancers among 3,220 people followed for 7 more years, with no link to replacement use; at least some forms of smokeless tobacco raise the risk of cancers of the mouth, oesophagus and pancreas, by less than smoking and without raising many smoking-related cancers, which the chapter reads as suggesting nicotine may not be a strong tumour promoter in people, while cautioning that oral and inhaled exposure differ). The chapter has no numbered conclusion on the heart (its text says it is likely that nicotine's effects on heart rate, heart contraction, resistance in the coronary vessels and insulin sensitivity contribute to some extent to the cardiovascular risk of people who smoke) or on dependence (it carries earlier reports forward: nicotine is the major chemical in tobacco responsible for dependence, the risk depends on how fast and how much nicotine is delivered, not all forms of nicotine delivery carry the same risk of dependence, nicotine replacement medicines designed to minimise it carry a low risk, and cigarettes have been designed to raise the likelihood of dependence through contents and emissions beyond nicotine). It also reports modest thinking-enhancing effects of acute nicotine in adults who smoke during withdrawal (and, in its evidence summary, in adults who do not smoke), with little known about long-term effects; that authors with industry funding reported positive findings on nicotine and thinking almost exclusively, as cited; that the long-term effects of nicotine, compared with smoking and with no tobacco use, still need study; and that all tobacco products contain toxicants and so carry some health risk. Not measured: the share of smoking's harm that is due to nicotine, and long-term outcomes in people who use nicotine without smoke. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.population: People and laboratory animals exposed to nicotine on its own (as medicine, in smokeless tobacco or in experiments), and people who smoke, as reviewed in the US Surgeon General's 2014 report
claims.exposure: Nicotine on its own, without the other substances in tobacco smoke
claims.comparator: Burning tobacco (cigarette smoke), and no tobacco or nicotine use
claims.outcome: Acute poisoning; disease-related biological pathways; fetal brain and lung development and pregnancy outcomes; adolescent brain development; cancer; heart disease; dependence; each as graded or described by the report
claims.magnitude: No effect size is given for most conclusions. Where cited: Swedish population study 1999 to 2010, snus and small-for-gestational-age term births, adjusted odds ratio 1.21 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.43), smaller than for smoking (the smoking figure is printed as 2.27 with an interval of 2.62 to 2.91, a misprint because the estimate lies outside its own interval, so it is not quoted); preterm delivery 27% higher with smoking (Shah and Bracken 2000, as cited), with a rise of similar size for snus in Sweden; trial of nicotine patches in 250 pregnant women: birth weight 186 g higher (35 to 336), no difference in quit rates; Lung Health Study: 5,887 enrolled, 3,220 followed for 7 more years, 75 lung cancers, no link with nicotine replacement use. Grades: sufficient for 4 conclusions, suggestive but not sufficient for 1, inadequate for 1. The report apportions none of the harm between nicotine and smoke.
claims.reasoning: A description of what a narrative review concluded, seen only through that review. Observational and experimental evidence starts low (METHODS 6.3) and a claim seen only through reviews is downgraded for risk of bias (not appraisable: no search method, cited studies not appraised) and for indirectness (second-hand; nicotine on its own in people is mostly inferred from other products and from animals): very low, the floor. The relation is 'describes' because the claim reports the report's graded conclusions and not an effect of nicotine measured by the editors; the grades (sufficient, suggestive, inadequate) are the authors' judgments. Major Conclusion 9 is read as a statement about which products cause the burden, not as showing how much of the harm is due to smoke rather than nicotine, which the report does not apportion. Status single study: one report is the source and its figures come from primary studies that were not read. It stays draft because it rests only on a narrative review (METHODS 6.3 and 12).

current_lines.q: Is it the nicotine or the smoke that does the harm?
current_lines.short: Burned tobacco causes most of tobacco's harm, a big US report says. But it judges that nicotine on its own can still harm an unborn baby.
current_lines.but: It doesn't say how much of smoking's harm comes from nicotine itself. And the report sums up other studies, so this is second-hand.
how: A 2014 US Surgeon General's report says burned tobacco, like cigarettes, causes by far most of tobacco's death and disease in the US. That's about products. It doesn't split the harm between nicotine and the rest of the smoke.

For nicotine alone, it found enough evidence that it can poison in high enough amounts. It also judged that nicotine harms an unborn baby's growing brain and adds to early births and stillbirths. The brain finding comes from lab studies, the pregnancy one mostly from smokeless tobacco and patch trials.

For teenagers' brains, it called the evidence suggestive but not enough. For cancer, it was too thin to say either way. It made no ruling on the heart, but calls it likely that nicotine adds somewhat to heart risk in people who smoke.

It says nicotine is the main thing in tobacco that hooks people, but nicotine medicines carry a low risk of that. Nicotine gave a small boost to thinking in adults who smoke while in withdrawal, and in some who don't smoke. Authors paid by industry reported almost only good effects on thinking.
current_lines.rate: One big US government report that sums up other studies and doesn't say how it found them. For nicotine on its own, it leans mostly on animal studies and other products, with few studies of people using nicotine alone.

myth_or_fact_items.statement: Nicotine gum and patches hook people as much as smoking does.
myth_or_fact_items.why: A big US report says nicotine medicines carry a low risk of getting hooked. That's the report's judgment of other studies.

myth_or_fact_items.statement: It's been proven that nicotine on its own causes cancer.
myth_or_fact_items.why: A big US report found the evidence too thin to say either way. It says burned tobacco causes most of tobacco's harm.

lines_he_saw_on_13_november.q: Is it the nicotine or the smoke that does the harm?
lines_he_saw_on_13_november.short: Burning tobacco does most of the harm. Nicotine alone can still harm an unborn baby.
lines_he_saw_on_13_november.but: The report talks about products. It does not say how much of the harm comes from nicotine itself.
how: A 2014 US Surgeon General's report says most deaths and disease from tobacco come from burned tobacco.
For nicotine alone, it found enough proof that it is poisonous in large amounts, harms a baby's brain growth and adds to pregnancy problems.
The proof for the baby's brain comes from experiments, not from studies of people.
There is not enough evidence either way on nicotine and cancer. Its long-term effects still need study.

claims.statement: As summarized in the US Surgeon General's reports of 2006 and 2014 (narrative reviews that grade their conclusions; the figures are second-hand here, and the 2014 report builds on the 2006 one, so the two are not independent replication), people who do not smoke but breathe other people's tobacco smoke, compared with people who are not exposed, are linked to illness in the authors' graded judgments. In children (2006): sufficient to infer a causal relationship for sudden infant death syndrome, lower respiratory illness in infancy and early childhood (greatest from the mother's smoking), middle ear disease, cough, phlegm, wheeze and breathlessness and ever having asthma at school age, onset of wheeze illnesses in early childhood, lower lung function in childhood, and a small reduction in birth weight; suggestive but not sufficient for preterm delivery, onset of childhood asthma and several childhood cancers; inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship for fertility, spontaneous abortion, congenital malformations, and children's thinking and behaviour. In adults: sufficient for lung cancer in people who never smoked (pooled studies indicate a 20 to 30 percent higher risk from living with a person who smokes) and for coronary heart disease (pooled relative risks indicate a 25 to 30 percent higher risk), and for odour annoyance and nasal irritation; stroke was graded suggestive in 2006 and sufficient in 2014 (an increase of about 20 to 30%); several respiratory symptoms, adult-onset asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and breast cancer were graded suggestive, and others inadequate. The 2014 report adds that smokefree laws were followed by fewer coronary events in people under 65 (sufficient). The parts read give no relative or absolute risks for the children's outcomes or for adult outcomes other than lung cancer, coronary heart disease and stroke. The 2006 report states that there is no risk-free level of exposure to secondhand smoke; its chapter 1 gives no separate derivation or threshold analysis for the statement. By the editors' reading, the nearest reasoning in the part read is toxicological and mechanistic (more than 50 carcinogens in secondhand smoke; raised urinary levels of a tobacco-specific carcinogen's metabolites in people who do not smoke; a clot-promoting effect, harm to the lining of blood vessels and atherosclerosis in animals) together with the raised risks above and the report's statement that adults have immediate adverse effects on the cardiovascular system, while the report adds that the cancer risk is lower than from active smoking because the carcinogen dose is substantially lower and that, from what is known of dose and mechanisms, it anticipates only slightly or modestly raised risks for some associations, such as lung cancer. The report says exposure misclassification and near-universal background exposure may bias estimates toward no effect, that lifestyle differences may bias them the other way, and that uncertainty around pooled estimates may exceed what the statistics show; it also reports industry-linked criticism of the evidence. The chapters that review the evidence disease by disease (chapters 2 to 10 of the 2006 report), where any dose-response or low-exposure data would sit, were not read. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.population: Children and adults who do not smoke and are exposed to other people's tobacco smoke (secondhand smoke), as reviewed in the US Surgeon General's reports of 2006 (evidence to about 2005) and 2014
claims.exposure: Breathing other people's tobacco smoke (secondhand smoke), at home, at work and elsewhere
claims.comparator: People not exposed, or less exposed, to secondhand smoke, as defined in the studies the reports review (not read here)
claims.outcome: Death and disease in children and in adults who do not smoke: sudden infant death, respiratory illness, ear disease, asthma, lung function, birth weight, lung cancer, coronary heart disease and stroke; and whether any level of exposure is without risk
claims.magnitude: 2006 report, as summarized in its chapter 1: pooled studies indicate a 20 to 30 percent increase in the risk of lung cancer from secondhand smoke exposure associated with living with a person who smokes, and a 25 to 30 percent increase in the risk of coronary heart disease; 2014 report: an increase of about 20 to 30% in the risk of stroke. No relative risks, intervals or absolute risks are given in the part read for the children's outcomes or for the other adult outcomes; the size of the fall in coronary events after smokefree laws is not given in the conclusions. Grades by outcome as in the statement (sufficient, suggestive but not sufficient, inadequate). The 'no risk-free level' statement has no figure or threshold in the part read.
claims.reasoning: Findings of observational studies, biomarker and animal studies seen only through two narrative reviews. They start low (METHODS 6.3) and a claim seen only through reviews is downgraded for risk of bias (not appraisable) and indirectness (second-hand; the no-risk-free-level statement is supported only indirectly): very low, the floor. Very low here reflects how the claim is seen, not weak judgments by the reports, which grade many outcomes sufficient to infer a causal relationship. The relation is worded as an association; the causal wording belongs to the reports' own grades, which the statement attributes to them. Status single study: the 2014 report's secondhand smoke conclusions build on the 2006 report, so the two do not count as independent replication. The editors' reading of what the statement on a risk-free level rests on is labelled as theirs. It stays draft because it rests only on narrative reviews (METHODS 6.3 and 12). The 2006 report covers evidence to about 2005; the 2014 report updates stroke and adds smokefree law findings.

current_lines.short: Yes, two big US reports judge. It's linked to sudden infant death and asthma, and to 20 to 30% more lung cancer in adults who don't smoke.
current_lines.but: These are the reports' judgments of other studies, so the figures are second-hand. And the later report builds on the earlier one.
how: In children, the 2006 US Surgeon General's report found enough evidence that others' smoke causes sudden infant death. The same went for chest and ear illness, wheeze, asthma at school age, weaker lungs and a small drop in birth weight. For early birth and some childhood cancers, the evidence was suggestive but not enough.

In adults who don't smoke, it found enough evidence for lung cancer and heart disease. Living with someone who smokes went with a 20 to 30% higher lung cancer risk, and heart disease risk was 25 to 30% higher.
The 2014 report added stroke, with a risk about 20 to 30% higher. It also found that smoke-free laws were followed by fewer heart attacks and similar events in people under 65.

The 2006 report says no level of secondhand smoke is risk-free. The parts we read give no figures for that, and by our reading it rests mostly on lab findings. The report expects less cancer risk than from smoking, since people breathe in far less of the cancer-causing chemicals.
current_lines.rate: Two US government reports that sum up other studies, and the later builds on the earlier. We saw only their summaries, which is why the evidence counts as very limited here, not because the reports doubted the links.

myth_or_fact_items.statement: Breathing other people's smoke has been linked to sudden infant death.
myth_or_fact_items.why: A 2006 US Surgeon General's report found enough evidence to call it a cause. That's the report's judgment of other studies.

myth_or_fact_items.statement: After smoke-free laws came in, heart attacks fell in people under 65.
myth_or_fact_items.why: A 2014 US Surgeon General's report found enough evidence for fewer heart attacks and similar events in people under 65. That's the report's judgment, second-hand.

lines_he_saw_on_13_november.q: Does other people's smoke harm people nearby?
lines_he_saw_on_13_november.short: Other people's tobacco smoke is linked to illness in children and adults.
lines_he_saw_on_13_november.but: We read only the summary chapters of two US reports, and the later one builds on the earlier one.
how: In children, a 2006 US report found enough proof of links with sudden infant death, chest and ear infections, wheeze and asthma.
In adults who don't smoke, it found enough proof of links with lung cancer (risk 20 to 30 percent higher) and heart disease (25 to 30 percent).
A 2014 report added stroke, and fewer heart attacks in people under 65 after smoke-free laws.
The 2006 report says no level of other people's smoke is risk-free. Its reasons come mostly from laboratory findings.

claims.statement: In a systematic review without pooling by four authors at the US Food and Drug Administration's Center for Tobacco Products (22 articles from 16 prospective cohorts published before June 2014; seen here only through the review, which has no protocol and does not appraise the bias of the studies), people who currently smoked only cigars, with no history of cigarette or pipe smoking ('primary' cigar smoking), compared with people who never smoked or never used tobacco, were associated with higher death rates from cancers of the mouth, oesophagus, larynx and lung, and slightly higher death rates from all causes and from coronary heart disease. The figures come mainly from two American Cancer Society cohorts, CPS-I (followed 1959 to 1972; 15,191 people who smoked only cigars) and CPS-II (followed 1982 to 1994, men only; 7,888): oral cancer 7.92 (95% CI 5.12 to 11.69) and 4.0 (1.5 to 10.3); oesophageal cancer 3.60 (2.17 to 5.62) and 1.8 (0.9 to 3.7); laryngeal cancer 10.02 (4.01 to 20.64) and 10.3 (2.6 to 41.0); lung cancer 2.1 (1.63 to 2.65) and 5.1 (4.0 to 6.6); all causes 1.08 (1.05 to 1.12) in CPS-I; coronary heart disease 1.05 (1.00 to 1.11) and, in men aged 30 to 74, 1.30 (1.05 to 1.62); bladder cancer and stroke were not clearly raised. Ratios generally rose with the number of cigars a day and with reported inhalation (not for oesophageal cancer in CPS-II). In CPS-I: all causes 1.02, 1.08 and 1.17 for 1 to 2, 3 to 4 and 5 or more cigars a day, and 1.04, 1.19 and 1.60 for no, slight and moderate-to-deep inhalation; lung cancer 0.9 (0.54 to 1.66), 2.36 and 3.4 by the same amounts. In CPS-II: lung cancer 1.3 (0.7 to 2.4) at 1 to 2 and 7.8 (5.9 to 10.3) at 3 or more cigars a day, and 3.3 (2.3 to 4.7) without inhalation against 11.3 (7.9 to 16.1) with it. Among people reporting no inhalation, the ratios for cancers of the mouth, oesophagus and larynx were still raised in CPS-I (6.98, 3.4 and 10.6) but their intervals include 1 in CPS-II (3.2, 1.6 and 4.2). People with an earlier history of cigarette or pipe smoking ('secondary' cigar smoking) had higher ratios for lung cancer (6.29 against 2.1) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (4.39 against 1.42) in CPS-I. Studies that combined cigars and pipes pointed the same way (all causes 1.09 to 1.37 in people with no history of cigarette smoking, each interval starting at 0.98 or higher). The authors describe two other studies of cancer cases, the EPIC cohort and the INHANCE pooled analysis of head and neck cancer, as consistent with these results (not read). The review excludes people who currently smoke cigarettes and tabulates no estimates for them, so it does not show whether cigar smoking is more or less harmful than cigarette smoking, although its authors write that some cigar risks can be as high as or exceed those of cigarette smoking, especially at the highest amounts and levels of inhalation. For scale only, and not as a comparison made by either study: in a separate US survey cohort of 1997 to 2004 (Jha et al.), men who currently smoked cigarettes had 2.8 times the all-cause death rate and 14.6 times the lung cancer death rate of men who had smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in their lives (a different era, adjustment and comparison group from the cigar cohorts). The cohorts began between the 1940s and the 1980s and were largely white men in North America and Europe who smoked large cigars; most estimates are adjusted for age alone; no ratios were pooled; women, non-white people, younger adults and today's cigar products (varied shapes, sizes, tips and filters) are not covered, and studies were often too small to detect effects at the lowest amounts; and the review reports no absolute risks. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.population: People in 16 prospective cohorts enrolled from the 1940s to the 1980s, largely white men in North America and Europe who smoked large cigars; mainly two American Cancer Society cohorts (CPS-I, 15,191 people who smoked only cigars; CPS-II, men only, 7,888)
claims.exposure: Currently smoking cigars only, with no history of cigarette or pipe smoking ('primary'); also with such a history ('secondary'); by cigars a day, self-reported inhalation and years of smoking
claims.comparator: People who never smoked or never used tobacco; people who currently smoke cigarettes are excluded by design and no cigarette estimates are tabulated
claims.outcome: Death from any cause and from cancers of the mouth, oesophagus, larynx, lung, pancreas and bladder, coronary heart disease, stroke, aortic aneurysm and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
claims.magnitude: Primary cigar smoking against never smoking or never using tobacco, mortality ratios (95% CI), CPS-I / CPS-II: all causes 1.08 (1.05 to 1.12; 3,754 deaths) / not tabulated; oral cancer 7.92 (5.12 to 11.69) / 4.0 (1.5 to 10.3); oesophageal 3.60 (2.17 to 5.62) / 1.8 (0.9 to 3.7); laryngeal 10.02 (4.01 to 20.64) / 10.3 (2.6 to 41.0); lung 2.1 (1.63 to 2.65) / 5.1 (4.0 to 6.6); pancreatic 1.62 (1.22 to 2.11) / 1.3 (0.9 to 1.9); bladder 1.38 (0.89 to 2.04) / 1.0 (0.4 to 2.3); coronary heart disease 1.05 (1.00 to 1.11) / 1.30 (1.05 to 1.62) in men 30 to 74 and 0.93 (0.72 to 1.21) at 75 and over; stroke 0.96 (0.87 to 1.06) in CPS-I; aortic aneurysm 1.76 (1.29 to 2.35) in CPS-I; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 1.42 (0.96 to 2.03) in CPS-I. By cigars a day (1 to 2 / 3 to 4 / 5 or more), CPS-I: all causes 1.02 / 1.08 / 1.17; oral cancer 2.12 / 8.51 / 15.94; lung 0.9 / 2.36 / 3.4; CPS-II (1 to 2 / 3 or more): lung 1.3 / 7.8, oesophageal 1.8 / 1.9 (no gradient). Reporting no inhalation, CPS-I / CPS-II: oral 6.98 (4.13 to 11.03) / 3.2 (0.9 to 11.0); oesophageal 3.4 (1.90 to 5.61) / 1.6 (0.7 to 4.1); laryngeal 10.6 (3.87 to 23.07) / 4.2 (0.5 to 37.1). claims.reasoning: Observational cohorts seen only through a systematic review without pooling, so the claim starts low. Downgraded once for risk of bias (the review is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2, the studies are mostly adjusted for age alone, cigarette history and inhalation are self-reported, and the tables have mismatches) and once for indirectness (second-hand; old cohorts of largely men smoking large cigars). Upgraded for a large effect (several ratios of 4 to 10 for mouth and larynx cancer and 5 for lung cancer, still large in the model adjusted for alcohol and smokeless tobacco) and for a dose-response gradient (cigars a day, inhalation and years of smoking for the four cancers), the upgrades being applied to evidence already rated down for risk of bias; a strict reading, without the upgrades, would give very low, and the gap between the two is the possibility that people who reported never smoking cigarettes had in fact smoked them, which would inflate the ratios and which the dose gradients argue against but do not exclude. The rating applies to the cancers; the all-cause ratio (1.08), coronary heart disease (1.05 and 1.30), the no-inhalation ratios, the low-amount ratios and the juxtaposed cigarette figures are less certain and, taken alone, would be rated very low. Status replicated for the cancers: besides the two American Cancer Society cohorts, which share a research programme and are not independent of each other, the Dorn study, the Swedish census cohort and the Copenhagen City Heart Study give ratios in the same direction for lung cancer, and the Dorn study for mouth and larynx cancer (their estimates are for current cigar smoking whatever the earlier cigarette history, so earlier cigarette smoking can inflate them). The review's authors work for the regulator of tobacco products and declare no competing interests; no funding statement is printed. The claim does not say that cigars are more or less harmful than cigarettes, which the review does not test.

current_lines.short: It seems so. In big US studies, people who smoked only cigars died of mouth cancer 4 to 8 times as often as people who never smoked.
current_lines.but: The studies began decades ago, mostly with white men who smoked big cigars. And the review didn't compare them with cigarettes.
how: A review by four staff at the US Food and Drug Administration looked at 16 long-running studies. They began between the 1940s and the 1980s. It compared people who smoked only cigars, never cigarettes or pipes, with people who never used tobacco.

Most figures come from two big American Cancer Society studies. Deaths from mouth cancer were about 4 to 8 times as common, from voice-box cancer about 10 times, and from lung cancer 2 to 5 times. Deaths from any cause were only slightly higher.

Risks mostly rose with more cigars a day and with inhaling the smoke. In the older study, even people who said they didn't inhale had more deaths from cancers of the mouth, gullet and voice box. The newer one had too few to be sure.

The review left out people who smoke cigarettes, so it can't show whether cigars are less or more harmful. Its authors still wrote that some cigar risks can be as high as cigarettes' or higher, which their tables can't show.
current_lines.rate: The links are big and grew with more cigars, which helps. But the studies are old, mostly of white men, took little but age into account, and come through one review that didn't judge their quality.

myth_or_fact_items.statement: If you don't inhale, cigars don't raise your risk of mouth cancer.
myth_or_fact_items.why: In one big old US study, people who said they didn't inhale still died more often of mouth, gullet and voice-box cancer than people who never smoked. A second study had too few to be sure.

lines_he_saw_on_13_november.q: What do cigars do to health?
lines_he_saw_on_13_november.short: Smoking cigars is linked to more deaths from mouth, throat and lung cancer than never smoking.
lines_he_saw_on_13_november.but: The studies are old, mostly of men, and did not compare cigars with cigarettes.
how: A review by US Food and Drug Administration staff looked at people who smoked only cigars, against people who never smoked.
In the two biggest studies, deaths from mouth cancer were about 4 to 8 times as common, and from lung cancer 2 to 5 times.
Risks mostly rose with more cigars a day, and with breathing the smoke in.
The review did not rate how good the studies were. They began between the 1940s and the 1980s.

claims.statement: In Swedish men who had never smoked, snus use compared with using no tobacco is associated with a higher rate of death from any cause in the largest pooled cohort analysis read here (eight cohorts, 169,103 men, 10,928 deaths, about 17 years of follow-up on average, editors' calculation): adjusted for age and body mass index only, the hazard ratio for men who used snus and no other tobacco was 1.28 (95% CI 1.20–1.35), for cardiovascular deaths 1.27 (1.15–1.41), for cancer deaths 1.12 (1.00–1.26) and for deaths from other causes 1.37 (1.24–1.52) (Byhamre et al., 2021; funded by a university department, Swedish regional authorities and a medical society; no conflicts declared). The paper prints deaths by group but no rates per person-year, and the groups differed (men who used snus were younger, mean age 29 against 38, and more often in the highest alcohol tertile, 37.9% against 20.2%), so the ratios cannot be turned into a number out of 100. The ratio rose with years of use (1.08 under 5 years, 1.29 at 15 years or more) but not clearly with weekly amount; it was 1.42 (1.21–1.66) without the construction-worker cohort, which supplied 87% of the deaths in the snus group (editors' arithmetic); and the cardiovascular ratio was 1.13 (0.93–1.38) with follow-up capped at 10 years, which the authors say calls for caution. For cancers, an independent systematic review of 15 studies that left out work linked to the tobacco industry (Valen et al., 2023; no funding statement on the page; no conflicts declared) gave, in its summary table and per 100,000 men (the snus figure being the no-tobacco figure with the hazard ratio applied), oesophageal squamous cell cancer 16 with no tobacco and 55 with snus (HR 3.5, 1.6–7.6; one cohort, 10 exposed cases), pancreatic cancer at 27 years 72 and 151 (RR 2.1, 1.2–3.3; 18 exposed cases), and cancer deaths 2,141 and 2,395, which is 2.1 and 2.4 in 100 men (editors' conversion; the row comes from Byhamre et al.), with raised ratios also for non-cardia stomach cancer (HR 1.4, 1.1–1.9) and rectal cancer (1.38, 1.07–1.77). Its authors rated these moderate certainty for the oesophagus and for the pancreas at 27 years and low for the others; the pancreatic ratio was 1.07 (0.77–1.50) in a pooled analysis over 36 years (very low), the rectal ratio 1.10 (0.91–1.34) with longer follow-up, and oral cancer (0.93, 0.59–1.44), lung cancer (0.8, 0.4–1.3) and colon cancer (1.08, 0.91–1.29) showed no clear difference. A narrative review supported by Swedish Match, a snus maker, and written by a long-term consultant to the tobacco industry (Lee, 2013) concluded that adverse health effects of snus have not been clearly identified and that any cancer risk is at most minimal and much less than that of smoking; it pooled heart attack in never-smoking Swedish men to RR 1.07 (0.98–1.16), or 1.00 (0.91–1.10) without one 1971–74 estimate, while its own results also show fatal heart attack 1.31 (1.09–1.58) against non-fatal 0.89 (0.79–1.00), heart failure up to 2.08 (1.03–4.22), and poorer survival after a cancer diagnosis in men who used snus only (1.13, 1.05–1.20), though less so than in men who smoked only (1.21, 1.17–1.25). IARC (2012) judged smokeless tobacco as a class carcinogenic to humans (Group 1: oral cavity, oesophagus, pancreas) without separating products, and notes that Swedish snus is made with extra controls on nitrosamines and that four northern-European studies of oral cancer found no overall association. A 2026 systematic review without meta-analysis, rated critically low confidence by the editors (Kopa-Stojak & Pawliczak, 2026), describes pooled heart attack, stroke, atrial fibrillation and pancreatic cancer estimates near 1 (1.04, 1.04, 1.07, 0.96) beside fatal heart attack 1.28 (1.06–1.55) and heart failure 2.08 (1.03–4.22). Against smoking the sources give little: Byhamre et al. left out men who had ever regularly smoked; Valen et al. report cancer estimates higher for smoking than for snus at most sites in the same studies, with overlapping intervals except for lung (Figure 4, not read as numbers), and say it is not known how far switching from smoking to snus reduces the benefit of stopping all tobacco; no source read compares the overall death rate of men who use snus with that of people who smoke, and the figure of no more than 1% of the effects of smoking in Lee's Discussion comes from his 2011 review, which was not read. These sources overlap heavily (the Swedish construction-worker cohort sits inside most estimates), tobacco use was recorded once at the start, women are almost absent, few men were followed beyond 70, and none of these studies can show that snus caused the differences. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.population: Men in Sweden who had never smoked, in cohorts recruited from the 1970s to 2010 (one dominant construction-worker cohort), with Norwegian cohort data in IARC's review, and in reviews of such studies; no data on women beyond one lymphoma estimate
claims.exposure: Using snus (moist smokeless tobacco as made in Sweden), recorded once at the start of each study; mostly snus with no other tobacco
claims.comparator: Men who never used any tobacco (the main comparison in every study read); men who formerly used snus; men who smoked (indirect, from the few comparisons within the same studies)
claims.outcome: Death from any cause, from cardiovascular disease and from cancer; cancers of the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas and rectum; heart attack and heart failure; survival after a cancer diagnosis; and what IARC concludes for smokeless tobacco as a class
claims.magnitude: Byhamre et al. 2021 (eight Swedish cohorts; never-smoking men; 124,256 never used tobacco, 39,156 current snus only, 5,691 former snus only; adjusted for attained age and body mass index): current snus only against never used, all-cause HR 1.28 (1.20–1.35; 1,410 deaths against 9,272), cardiovascular 1.27 (1.15–1.41; 443 against 3,444), cancer 1.12 (1.00–1.26; 332 against 2,660), other causes 1.37 (1.24–1.52; 511 against 2,098) (the groups differ in age, so death counts are not comparable between them; no absolute rates are printed); former snus only: all-cause 1.15 (1.02–1.31), cancer 1.26 (1.01–1.57), cardiovascular 1.13 (0.91–1.41), other causes 1.14 (0.89–1.45). By years of use, all-cause under 5 years 1.08 (0.88–1.32), 5–9 1.17 (1.00–1.36), 10–14 1.31 (1.12–1.52), 15 or more 1.29 (1.20–1.38), p for trend 0.001; by weekly amount 1.28, 1.17, 1.37, p for trend 0.09. Sensitivity: without the Construction Worker Cohort 1.42 (1.21–1.66), cardiovascular 1.39 (1.05–1.84), cancer 1.52 (1.15–1.99); follow-up capped at 10 years 1.34 (1.21–1.48), cardiovascular 1.13 (0.93–1.38); extra adjustment for education, alcohol and physical activity in six cohorts (158 snus-group deaths) 1.46 (1.22–1.75). Valen et al. 2023 (snus only against no tobacco; absolute risks per 100,000 men over each study's follow-up as in the review's table, no tobacco then snus, the snus figure being the no-tobacco figure with the hazard ratio applied): oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 16 then 55, HR 3.5 (1.6–7.6), moderate; pancreas at 27 years 72 then 151, RR 2.1 (1.2–3.3 in the table, 1.2–3.6 in the text), moderate, and HR 1.07 (0.77–1.50) at 36 years, very low; non-cardia stomach 237 then 332, HR 1.4 (1.1–1.9), low; rectum 339 then 468, HR 1.38 (1.07–1.77), low, and 1.10 (0.91–1.34) with longer follow-up; cancer deaths 2,141 then 2,395 (2.1 then 2.4 in 100 men, editors' conversion), HR 1.12 (1.00–1.26), low; oral cancer 0.93 (0.59–1.44), very low; lung RR 0.8 (0.4–1.3); colon HR 1.08 (0.91–1.29); all melanoma incidence rate ratio 0.65 (0.52–0.82). After a cancer diagnosis in construction workers: total mortality HR 1.13 (1.05–1.20), cancer death 1.15 (1.05–1.26). Lee 2013 (never-smoking Swedish men): heart attack or ischaemic heart disease, 13 estimates pooled, fixed-effect RR 1.07 (0.98–1.16), 1.00 (0.91–1.10) without the 1971–74 estimate; fatal heart attack 1.31 (1.09–1.58), non-fatal 0.89 (0.79–1.00); heart failure 1.28 (1.00–1.64; 75 exposed cases) and 2.08 (1.03–4.22; 14 cases); survival after a cancer diagnosis, all-cause RR 1.13 (1.05–1.20) snus only, 1.21 (1.17–1.25) smoking only, 1.17 (1.12–1.22) both; cancer-specific 1.15 (1.05–1.26) against 1.15 (1.10–1.21). IARC 2012: smokeless tobacco Group 1; northern-Europe oral cancer pooled 1.0 (0.7–1.3); Swedish oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma RR 3.5 (1.6–7.6); pancreas Norway 1.67 (1.12–2.50; 45 cases; 0.85, 0.24–3.07, in people who never smoked) and Swedish construction workers 2.1 (1.2–3.6; 18 cases), pooled 1.8 (1.3–2.5). Kopa-Stojak 2026 (as described, from primary analyses): heart attack 1.04 (0.93–1.17); fatal heart attack 1.28 (1.06–1.55); stroke 1.04 (0.92–1.17), death after stroke 1.32 (1.08–1.61); atrial fibrillation 1.07 (0.97–1.19); heart failure 2.08 (1.03–4.22) and 1.28 (1.00–1.64); cardiovascular death 1.70 (1.01–2.87) in people who used snus and never used tobacco; pancreatic cancer 0.96 (0.83–1.11) pooled against 2.0 (1.2–3.3) in one cohort; rectal cancer 1.40 (1.09–1.79).
claims.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is downgraded one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor, so very low. Rated as worded: an association in never-smoking men, snus only against no tobacco; whether it is causal is a separate and unresolved question. The ratings in the Valen et al. review (moderate for the oesophagus and for the pancreas at 27 years, low for stomach, rectum and cancer deaths, very low for most others) are its authors' judgments from a different starting point and are reported, not adopted. Overlapping reports are counted once: the Swedish construction-worker cohort sits inside Byhamre et al., Valen et al., Lee, IARC and Kopa-Stojak, Valen et al.'s mortality row is the Byhamre analysis, and the survival-after-cancer result in Lee and in Valen et al. is the same study, so the agreement between them is not independent replication and the status is contested, not replicated.

current_lines.short: It may be. Among Swedish men who never smoked, those who used snus died at a rate about 28% higher than men who used no tobacco.
current_lines.but: This can't show snus caused it: men who used snus also drank more. And no source we read compared their overall death rate with people who smoke.
how: The biggest study pooled eight Swedish groups of men who had never smoked: 169,103 men, followed for about 17 years. Those who used snus died at a rate about 28% higher than men who used no tobacco, taking only age and weight into account.

Men who used snus drank more, and the main result didn't take drinking into account. The gap grew with the years men had used snus. One group of construction workers gave most of the deaths, and leaving it out made the gap bigger, not smaller.

An independent cancer review, which left out tobacco-industry work, estimated gullet cancer at about 55 in 100,000 men who used snus, against 16 who used no tobacco. Cancer deaths were about 2.4 in 100, against 2.1. Mouth and lung cancer showed no clear difference.

A review paid for by a snus maker found no clear harm; its author has long advised tobacco firms. A world cancer agency rates smokeless tobacco as a whole as causing cancer. It notes that Swedish snus is made to keep some cancer-causing chemicals low.
current_lines.rate: Studies of Swedish men, most from one group of construction workers, with snus use asked once. Men who used snus also drank more, and the sources disagree; one of them was paid for by a snus maker.

myth_or_fact_items.statement: Swedish snus has been shown to raise the risk of mouth cancer.
myth_or_fact_items.why: In an independent review, mouth cancer showed no clear difference between men who used snus and men who used no tobacco. A world cancer agency rates smokeless tobacco as a whole as causing cancer, without rating snus on its own.

myth_or_fact_items.statement: Snus has been linked to cancer of the gullet.
myth_or_fact_items.why: An independent review estimated about 55 cases in 100,000 men who used snus, against 16 in men who used no tobacco. This can't show snus caused it.

lines_he_saw_on_13_november.q: What does snus do to health?
lines_he_saw_on_13_november.short: Among Swedish men who never smoked, snus was linked to a higher death rate than no tobacco.
lines_he_saw_on_13_november.but: These studies can't show that snus caused it, and none compared snus with smoking for deaths overall.
how: Men who used snus died at a rate about 28% higher than men who used no tobacco.
Cancers of the gullet and pancreas were rare, but more frequent in men who used snus. Mouth and lung cancer showed no clear difference.
A review supported by a snus maker found no clear harm; independent studies found the raised figures.
Nearly all the men were Swedish, and men who used snus drank more alcohol.

claims.statement: Nicotine pouches (tobacco-free oral pouches) have been measured in laboratories and surveys far more than in people. Laboratory analyses found nicotine in all the products sold as containing it, in very different amounts, and tobacco-specific nitrosamines absent or in small amounts, well below the amounts reported for snus. An independent German government laboratory (Mallock et al., 2024; intramural funding, no competing interests declared) analysed one pouch of each of 46 products from 20 producers bought online in 2021 (a convenience sample): the 44 that contained nicotine held 1.79 to 47.5 mg per pouch (median 9.48), and the nitrosamine NNN was found in 24 of them (9 below the quantification limit), at most 12.9 ng per pouch; the authors set this beside up to 1,190 ng NNN per pouch of snus and 33 to 323 ng per cigarette in smoke, figures from other studies on other bases. A study designed, interpreted and written by Swedish Match, maker of ZYN pouches and General snus, whose four authors are its employees (Back et al., 2023), found no nitrosamine above its quantification limit (0.01 µg/g, roughly 4 to 8 ng per pouch by the editors' arithmetic) in two ZYN variants, one batch each, against NNN 0.44 and NNK 0.19 µg/g in General snus in the same study, and quantified 4 or 5 of 43 compounds (nicotine included) in ZYN against 19 in snus. A 2026 scoping review (Travis et al., 2026) lists three further analyses: 1.41 to 8.11 mg per pouch in 70 US products, 6.4 against 12.3 mg in tobacco-based pouches in 50, and 2.20 to 56 mg in 31 sold in Germany, with measured nicotine generally at or below the label. In surveys, use is low but rising. In the US, current use among young people in 2024 was 1.8 in 100 (National Youth Tobacco Survey, middle and high school; 0.8 in 100 in 2021) and 2.6 in 100 (Monitoring the Future, grades 10 and 12; 1.3 in 100 in 2023; most also vaped), but 0.2 in 100 among 12- to 17-year-olds in the PATH study in 2022–23; among adults in 2022–23 it was 0.4 to 0.8 in 100; elsewhere current use ranged from 0.4 in 100 (adults in England, 2023) to 19 in 100 (youth and adults in Australia, 2023), from surveys of different kinds. Use was more likely in males, younger people and people who currently or formerly smoked, vaped or used smokeless tobacco; US sales rose from 327 to 1,046 million units between July 2021 and May 2024. In people, pouches have been followed for 6 months at most. A 2026 systematic review without meta-analysis (Kopa-Stojak & Pawliczak, 2026; critically low confidence by the editors) found 15 pouch studies, none following disease or death. In a non-industry-funded German crossover study of adults who smoked daily (as described by the scoping review), a 30 mg pouch gave more nicotine than a cigarette and 20 mg and 6 mg pouches less, and the 20 mg and 30 mg pouches raised systolic blood pressure and arterial stiffness comparably to a cigarette; industry-funded series found 4 mg and 8 mg pouches below a cigarette and, in people who used snus, pouches giving more nicotine than snus, and nicotine peaked later with pouches (20 to 42 minutes) than with a cigarette (5 to 7). In a small US survey sample, nicotine breakdown products in people who used only pouches were comparable to those in people who smoked, with lower cadmium and uranium; in a 4-week trial, nitrosamine levels were not lowered in people who cut their cigarettes with pouches. Oral findings were compared in small studies: oral lesions in 79 in 100 young Swedish adults who used pouches against 89 in 100 who used snus (a cross-sectional comparison of 126 and 63 people), and less gum inflammation after 24 weeks in an Altria-funded trial of adults who switched from smoking to pouches than in those who kept smoking. The scoping review's authors say the health effects remain largely understudied, that evidence of short-term benefit from switching is limited and mainly industry-funded, and that pouches may be a less hazardous alternative to traditional tobacco but are not risk-free. No source read follows heart disease, cancer, lung disease or death in people who use pouches, or compares them with people who use no nicotine on any health outcome; the product analyses read come from Germany, the United States and a few other countries, and the independent one bought its products in 2021. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (the contents and survey findings).
claims.population: Tobacco-free nicotine pouches on sale in Germany (46 products bought online in 2021), the United States and other countries; people who use them in national surveys (US youth and adults 2021 to 2024, other countries), crossover studies of 30 to 42 adults and small trials of 30 to 100 adults; a 2026 scoping review of 135 studies to September 2025
claims.exposure: Nicotine pouches: measured product contents; use as reported in surveys; short-term effects in single sessions up to 6 months of follow-up
claims.comparator: Snus; cigarettes; nicotine gum and lozenges; people who use no nicotine (the last not compared on any health outcome in the sources read)
claims.outcome: Measured nicotine, nitrosamine and other constituents; how many people use pouches and who they are; short-term nicotine uptake, blood pressure, arterial stiffness and biomarkers; health outcomes in people (none beyond 6 months, none for disease or death)
claims.magnitude: Mallock et al. 2024 (46 products, 20 producers, bought online January–May 2021; 44 with nicotine, 2 nicotine-free): nicotine 1.79–47.5 mg per pouch, median 9.48 (interquartile range 5.50–16.6), two above 40 mg; median extract pH 8.8 (range 5.5–10.5); printed milligram content on 15 of 44, a score or word on 38, none on 4; tobacco-specific nitrosamines found in 26 of 44: NNN in 24 (9 below the quantification limit of about 0.4 ng), NNK in 3, NAT in 6, NAB in 5; highest per pouch NNN 12.9 ng, NNK 5.4, NAT 2.7, NAB 5.6 (one pouch per product, single analysis); for comparison the authors cite up to 1,190 ng NNN and 120 ng NNK per pouch of snus, 2 ng NNN per gram of nicotine gum and 33–323 ng NNN and 40–246 ng NNK per cigarette in smoke (other studies, other bases). Back et al. 2023 (Swedish Match; 7 products, one batch each): nitrosamines none of ten above quantification limits (0.01 µg/g for NNN, NNK, NAT, NAB) in two ZYN variants and two nicotine replacement products; General snus NNN 0.44, NNK 0.19 µg/g; moist snuff NNN 3.63 and 2.53, NNK 2.27 and 0.92; compounds quantified (nicotine included) of 43: lozenge 2, ZYN moist 4, ZYN dry 5, gum 9, snus 19, moist snuff 26 and 27; ZYN dry and moist formaldehyde 10.3 and 1.5, chromium 0.160 and 0.099, ammonia 62 and 66 µg/g, nickel 0.067 in the dry variant only; total nicotine mg/g ZYN dry 7.63, ZYN moist 12.00, snus 8.13, lozenge 3.20, gum 1.30. Travis et al. 2026 as described (135 studies to September 2025; no risk-of-bias assessment): US 70 tobacco-free products 1.41–8.11 mg per pouch; 50 pouches 6.4 (SD 3.5) against 12.3 (SD 8.2) mg in tobacco-based pouches, free-base share 63.4% against 47.2%; 31 pouches in Germany 2.20–56 mg. US youth current use: National Youth Tobacco Survey (middle and high school) 0.8% (2021) to 1.8% (2024), lifetime 1.9% to 3.5%; Monitoring the Future (grades 10 and 12) 1.3% (2023) to 2.6% (2024), lifetime 3% to 5.4%; PATH ages 12–17 (2022–23) lifetime 0.9%, current 0.2%; of adolescents currently using in 2024, 29% frequent and 22% daily. US adults 2022–23: PATH lifetime 3.3%, current 0.8%; TUS-CPS 2.7% and 0.4%. Other countries, lifetime (current): British youth 2024 3.3% (1.2%); Quebec adolescents 3.7% (2.6%); Australia 2023 26% (19%); Finland 2022 14.4% (3.7%); Poland adults 2024 9.2% (4.3%); Canadian college students 2024 27% (12%); England adults 2023 current 0.4%. Nicotine uptake: independent German crossover 30 mg > cigarette > 20 mg > 6 mg (peak and total over 4 hours; time to peak 5 minutes for the cigarette, 20 minutes for the 6 mg pouch); industry series 4 mg and 8 mg below a cigarette, 12 mg and 8 mg mini comparable or higher, time to peak 35–40 minutes against 5–7; in adults using snus, 6, 9 and 11.2 mg pouches gave higher peak and 60-minute nicotine than 11.2 mg snus. 20 mg and 30 mg pouches raised systolic pressure and arterial stiffness comparably to a cigarette. Sales 327 million units (July 2021) to 1,046 million (May 2024). Kopa-Stojak 2026: 15 pouch studies, longest follow-up 6 months, none on disease or death; crossover trials of 30–42 adults; a 6-month online cohort (n = 1,863 at start) quitting odds 1.29 (1.04–1.59) for fruit-flavoured and 1.04 (0.82–1.28) for mint-flavoured pouches; Saudi surveys without comparison groups (for example bloating 66.7%, difficulty breathing 40.5%).
claims.reasoning: Descriptive evidence starts low like other observational evidence and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. The claim is worded as a description of measurements (contents, prevalence, short-term measures) and of what has not been measured (disease or death, anything beyond 6 months), not as an effect of pouches on health, so it is rated as worded and not upgraded for a large effect. Status replicated applies to the contents and survey findings, shown by independent laboratories and surveys that agree in direction (the independent German laboratory, the maker's laboratory and the analyses described by the scoping review; US national surveys); it does not apply to health effects, for which there is no evidence beyond short studies. Overlapping reports are counted once: the systematic review and the scoping review share some primary studies (for example two crossover trials and the oral-health trial), the systematic review cites both laboratory papers read here and the scoping review cites neither.

current_lines.short: Nobody knows yet. No study has followed people who use them for more than 6 months, or looked at disease or death.
current_lines.but: Most of what's known comes from lab tests and surveys, not from people's health. And the products differ a lot.
how: An independent German government lab tested 46 pouch products bought online in 2021, and 44 held nicotine. The amount varied a lot, and only 15 printed it in milligrams; 4 gave no sign of strength at all.

Traces of nitrosamines, cancer-causing chemicals from tobacco, turned up in 26 of the 44. Levels were far below those reported for snus. A pouch maker's own study found none above its test limit in two of its pouches.

In the US, about 2 in 100 middle and high school students used pouches in 2024, up from under 1 in 100 in 2021. Among adults it was under 1 in 100. Use was more common in males, younger people and people who smoked, vaped or used other tobacco.

Studies in people have lasted 6 months at most, and none looked at disease or death. In one small German study, as a review describes it, the two strongest pouches raised blood pressure and stiffened arteries about as much as a cigarette. That review's authors say pouches may be less harmful than tobacco but aren't risk-free.
current_lines.rate: Mostly lab tests of products and surveys of who uses them, not studies of health. The studies in people were small and short, and several were paid for by pouch or tobacco makers.

how: A German government laboratory found small amounts of cancer-linked chemicals in 26 of 44 pouches with nicotine, far below snus.

The latest review's authors say pouches may be less hazardous than traditional tobacco, but are not risk-free.

claims.statement: In people who smoked and were motivated to quit, in randomised and quasi-randomised trials comparing ways of using nicotine replacement (Cochrane review, search to April 2022; 16 trials with 12,169 people for combination use, 8 trials with 3,319 people for fast-acting forms against the patch), combination nicotine replacement (a patch plus a fast-acting form such as gum, lozenge, inhaler or nasal spray), compared with a single form, increased the number not smoking 6 months or more after the start of the quit attempt: about 4 more people in 100 (174 against 137 in 1,000, 95% CI 160 to 187; risk ratio 1.27, 1.17 to 1.37; I² 12%; people lost to follow-up counted as smoking). The ratio was similar against the patch alone (1.24, 1.13 to 1.37; 13 trials) and against a fast-acting form alone (1.30, 1.09 to 1.54; 6 trials); a third subgroup, one trial in which most people were lost to follow-up, gave a much larger ratio (5.16, 1.18 to 22.59). It was unchanged without the trials at high risk of bias, and a funnel plot of the 16 trials showed no sign of publication bias, which the authors read with caution because the number is small. A fast-acting form alone (lozenge, nasal spray, gum or inhaler), compared with the patch, showed no clear difference: 148 against 164 in 1,000, about 2 fewer in 100 with fast-acting forms (interval 4 fewer to 1 more; risk ratio 0.90, 0.77 to 1.05; I² 0%; 8 trials, one of them in adolescents; unchanged without the high-risk trials or the adolescent trial), with no clear difference for any single form (lozenge 0.94, 3 trials; nasal spray 0.90, 2 trials; gum 0.58, 2 trials and 118 people; inhaler 0.59, 1 trial and 222 people), so the interval does not rule out the patch doing somewhat better. People in these trials smoked about 20 or more cigarettes a day on average, so the results say little about lighter smoking; the review's comparisons of doses, lengths of use and timing, which gave mixed results, are not covered here. By the editors' count 9 of the 16 combination trials and 6 of the 8 fast-acting-against-patch trials named a manufacturer as funder, sponsor, supplier of product or employer of authors; the review judged company funding less relevant to comparisons between ways of using nicotine replacement and did not assess it. Certainty: high. Status: replicated.
claims.population: People who smoked and were motivated to quit, mostly smoking about 20 or more cigarettes a day, in randomised and quasi-randomised trials of ways of using nicotine replacement (68 trials, 43,327 people in the review; 16 trials, 12,169 people for combination use; 8 trials, 3,319 people for fast-acting forms against the patch); Cochrane review, search to April 2022
claims.exposure: Combination nicotine replacement (a patch plus a fast-acting form: gum, lozenge, inhaler or nasal spray); a fast-acting form alone
claims.comparator: A single form of nicotine replacement (patch alone, or a fast-acting form alone); for the fast-acting forms, the nicotine patch
claims.outcome: Not smoking 6 months or more after the start of the quit attempt (strictest definition, people lost to follow-up counted as smoking)
claims.magnitude: Combination vs single form: RR 1.27 (95% CI 1.17–1.37), I² 12%, 16 studies, 12,169 participants; 137 vs 174 per 1,000 (160–187), about 4 more in 100 (editors' subtraction: 37 per 1,000). Against patch alone 1.24 (1.13–1.37; 13 studies; 9,552; I² 28%); against a fast-acting form alone 1.30 (1.09–1.54; 6; 2,364; I² 0%); against a choice of single form 5.16 (1.18–22.59; 1 study; 253; high risk of bias). Fast-acting form vs patch: RR 0.90 (0.77–1.05), I² 0%, 8 studies, 3,319 participants; 164 vs 148 per 1,000 (126–172), about 2 fewer in 100 (interval 4 fewer to 1 more, editors' subtraction). By form: lozenge 0.94 (0.79–1.12; 3; 1,707), nasal spray 0.90 (0.64–1.27; 2; 1,272), gum 0.58 (0.26–1.31; 2; 118), inhaler 0.59 (0.22–1.60; 1; 222).
claims.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high, read through a Cochrane review (AMSTAR 2: high confidence, on the study card) whose two pools used here the review rates high. Risk of bias, not rated down: 9 of 68 trials were low risk in every domain and 28 high in at least one, but the review reports that restricting each pool to low-risk trials gave a consistent estimate and that removing high-risk trials changed the interpretation only for the timing comparison, which is outside this claim. Inconsistency, not rated down (I² 12% for combination use, 0% for fast-acting forms against the patch). Indirectness, not rated down: the claim is limited to people motivated to quit who smoked about 20 or more cigarettes a day in trials. Imprecision, not rated down: the combination interval (1.17 to 1.37) is far from no difference; the fast-acting-against-patch result is reported as no clear difference with its whole interval (0.77 to 1.05), which does not exclude a quit rate about a fifth lower with fast-acting forms, and the claim says so; the review's high rating rests on 3,319 people. Publication bias, not rated down: the funnel plot for combination use (16 trials) shows no asymmetry, though the authors caution that 16 is few, and the fast-acting-against-patch pool has too few trials for a funnel plot. The editors record that a manufacturer is linked to 9 of 16 combination trials and 6 of 8 fast-acting-against-patch trials (editors' count), that the review did not assess this, and that a stricter reading, taking company-linked trials as a possible source of inflation, would give moderate. Status replicated: the combination result is pooled from 16 trials by many groups with little heterogeneity. The 2018 review of nicotine replacement against control and this review may share trials (not checked); this claim rests on this review alone.

current_lines.q: Patch, gum or both: which works best for quitting smoking?
current_lines.short: A patch plus gum or similar did a little better. In trials, about 17 in 100 quit for 6 months or more, against 14 with one kind.
current_lines.but: The gain is small. And most people in these trials smoked about 20 or more cigarettes a day, so they say little about lighter smoking.
how: A Cochrane review pooled 16 trials with 12,169 people who wanted to quit. With a patch plus a quick form, like gum, a lozenge, an inhaler or a nose spray, 174 in 1,000 weren't smoking 6 months or more later, against 137 in 1,000 with one form. That's about 4 more in 100.

Both together did better than the patch alone and than a quick form alone, by about the same. The result held without the weakest trials, and a check found no sign of missing trials, though 16 is few for that check.
A quick form alone against the patch alone showed no clear difference: about 15 in 100 quit, against 16 in 100, in 8 trials. That doesn't rule out the patch doing somewhat better.

By our count, 9 of the 16 trials of both together had links to the products' makers, as funders, suppliers or employers. So did 6 of the 8 others. The review didn't check this, judging it mattered less when comparing ways of using the same products.
current_lines.rate: Strong: 16 trials comparing ways of using these products, with results that agree. One catch: over half had links to the products' makers, which the review didn't weigh.

myth_or_fact_items.statement: A nicotine patch plus gum or similar helped more people quit than one form alone.
myth_or_fact_items.why: In 16 trials, about 17 in 100 quit for 6 months or more with both, against 14 in 100 with one kind. The gain is small.

About 17 in 100 had stopped smoking after 6 months or more with a patch plus a fast-acting form, against about 14 in 100 with one form.
A fast-acting form alone and the patch alone showed no clear difference.

claims.statement: In people who smoked and joined trials of nicotine replacement for stopping smoking, chest pain or palpitations were reported more often with nicotine replacement than with placebo or no replacement: 2.5% against 1.4% (about 1 more in 100; odds ratio 1.88, 95% CI 1.37 to 2.57; the 15 trials that reported them, 11,074 people, including trials outside the review's main analysis; Cochrane review, search to July 2017). That review did not pool other side effects, because the trials reported them too differently, and lists them by form: with gum, hiccups, stomach upset, jaw pain and tooth or mouth problems; with the patch, skin irritation (up to 54% of people in one source it cites, usually mild); with the inhaler and sprays, irritation of the mouth, throat or nose, cough and runny nose; with sublingual tablets, hiccups, mouth burning, sore throat, cough, dry lips and mouth ulcers. Serious events were not pooled against placebo or no replacement: a patch trial in people with cardiovascular disease and six trials in pregnancy did not detect more serious events with nicotine replacement. In a later review comparing ways of using nicotine replacement (68 trials; search to April 2022), serious events were too few to compare (combination against a single form: 3 against 1 in 1,000, interval 1 to 18, seven events in total; risk ratio 4.44, 0.76 to 25.85; 5 trials, 2,888 people; low certainty), and more people stopped treatment because of side effects with fast-acting forms than with the patch (23 against 5 in 1,000; risk ratio 4.23, 1.54 to 11.63; 3 trials, 1,482 people; very low certainty), including 3.0% with a nasal spray against 0.9% with the patch in one trial of 922 people. All of this comes from treatment lasting weeks to months in people motivated to quit, so it cannot show how often rare serious events happen or what longer use does. Certainty: low (for the chest pain or palpitations result; the later review's figures carry its own lower ratings, and the lists of local effects are not graded). Status: mixed.
claims.population: People who smoked and joined trials of nicotine replacement for stopping smoking (136 studies in the 2018 review, chest pain or palpitations reported in 15 trials with 11,074 people; 68 trials in the 2023 review, serious events reported in 5 combination trials with 2,888 people), treated for weeks to months
claims.exposure: Nicotine replacement in any form (gum, patch, lozenge or tablet, inhaler, nasal or oral spray), alone or combined
claims.comparator: Placebo or no nicotine replacement; a single form of nicotine replacement; the nicotine patch (for fast-acting forms)
claims.outcome: Chest pain or palpitations; local side effects by form; serious adverse events; withdrawal from treatment because of side effects, as reported in the trials
claims.magnitude: Chest pain or palpitations: OR 1.88 (95% CI 1.37–2.57), 15 trials, 11,074 participants; 2.5% with NRT vs 1.4% with control (about 1 more in 100, editors' subtraction). An earlier meta-analysis cited by the review (12 studies) gave OR 2.06 (1.51–2.82) and overlaps these trials. Serious adverse events, combination vs single form: RR 4.44 (0.76–25.85), 5 trials, 2,888 participants; 1 vs 3 per 1,000 (1–18); seven events in total; low certainty. Withdrawals due to treatment: combination vs single form RR 1.12 (0.57–2.20; 5 trials; 3,070; I² 73%; 12 vs 14 per 1,000; very low); fast-acting form vs patch RR 4.23 (1.54–11.63; 3 trials; 1,482; 5 vs 23 per 1,000, 8–63; very low); nasal spray vs patch RR 3.47 (1.15–10.46; 1 trial; 922; 3.0% vs 0.9%). Serious events, fast-acting form vs patch: 3 of 4 trials (1,252 participants) had none; the fourth RR 1.75 (0.52–5.92; 642); very low certainty.
claims.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high; the rating is for the main finding, chest pain or palpitations, and the other figures in the statement are labelled with the lower ratings the 2023 review gave them. Risk of bias, one level: side effects were not defined, timed or collected in a common way (the 2018 review did not pool them because of extensive variation in reporting), the chest pain or palpitations result comes from the 15 trials that reported them out of 136, 43 trials had no matched placebo, and in the 2023 review two of the four or three trials behind the serious-event and withdrawal rows were at high risk of bias. Imprecision, one level: by the editors' arithmetic from the percentages, assuming equal group sizes, the chest pain or palpitations result has about 200 events, fewer than the 300 usually wanted, and serious events were so few (seven in the combination comparison) that the 2023 review took two levels. Inconsistency, not rated down for the main finding; the withdrawal figure for combination use has I² 73% and is labelled very low. Indirectness, not rated down: the claim is limited to what trials of nicotine replacement for stopping smoking recorded. An earlier meta-analysis of this outcome (12 studies, OR 2.06) overlaps these trials and is not counted as independent replication. Status mixed because most harm outcomes were too variably reported to pool, not because trials disagreed about chest pain or palpitations. The claim does not use figures from the cited network meta-analysis (not checked) or the 2023 review's comparisons of doses and timing, which are on that review's study card.

current_lines.q: What side effects do nicotine patches and gum have?
current_lines.short: Irritation where they're used, like skin for patches and the mouth for gum. Chest pain or a pounding heart: 2.5 in 100, against 1.4 without.
current_lines.but: These come from trials lasting weeks to months. Serious problems were too rare to compare.
how: Trials reported most side effects too differently to add up, so a Cochrane review listed them by form. Patches can irritate the skin, usually mildly, in up to 54 in 100 people in one source it cites. Gum can bring hiccups, stomach upset and jaw pain; inhalers and sprays can irritate the mouth, throat or nose.

In the 15 trials that counted them, with 11,074 people, chest pain or a pounding heart came up in 2.5 in 100 people on nicotine replacement, against 1.4 in 100 on a dummy or nothing. That's about 1 more in 100.

A patch trial in people with heart disease didn't find more serious problems with the patch. In a later review, serious problems were too few to compare a patch plus a quick form with one form: 7 in all, across 5 trials.

More people stopped a quick form, like gum or a nose spray, because of side effects than stopped the patch: about 23 against 5 in 1,000, in 3 trials, which is very uncertain. In one trial, 3 in 100 stopped a nose spray, against about 1 in 100 the patch.
current_lines.rate: Trials where chance decided who got nicotine, but they recorded side effects differently, and only 15 of 136 counted chest pain or a pounding heart, with fairly few cases. Serious problems were too rare to judge.

myth_or_fact_items.statement: Skin problems from nicotine patches are rare.
myth_or_fact_items.why: In one source a review cites, up to 54 in 100 people had skin irritation from patches, usually mild.

myth_or_fact_items.statement: Chest pain or a pounding heart was no more common on nicotine patches and gum.
myth_or_fact_items.why: In 15 trials, it came up in 2.5 in 100 people using them, against 1.4 in 100 on a dummy or nothing. Serious problems were too rare to compare.
