lines_he_saw_on_13_november.short: Side effects of nicotine patches and gum were mostly mild and local.
lines_he_saw_on_13_november.but: This comes from weeks to months of use in trials; serious problems were too few to judge.
how: Patches could irritate the skin. Gum, lozenges, sprays and inhalers could irritate the mouth, throat or nose.
Chest pain or palpitations: about 2.5 in 100 with nicotine replacement, against about 1.4 in 100 without.
More people stopped fast-acting forms because of side effects than the patch: about 23 against 5 in 1,000.

claims.statement: In adults who smoked cigarettes and joined randomised trials of nicotine vapes (80 trials, 29,861 people in the Cochrane living review, searched to 1 January 2026; 11 trials with 4,114 people compared with nicotine replacement and 7 trials with 1,918 people compared with vapes without nicotine; the trial supplied the vape in most), being given a nicotine vape, compared with nicotine replacement, increased the number not smoking at 6 months or longer: about 4 more people in 100 (10 against 6 in 100, interval 7 to 13; risk ratio 1.61, 95% CI 1.23 to 2.12; I² 55%); and, compared with a vape without nicotine, by about 2 more in 100 (8 against 6 in 100, interval 6 to 10; risk ratio 1.34, 1.05 to 1.69; I² 0%) (analysed as allocated, with people lost to follow-up counted as smoking). The 6 in 100 is the review's assumed quit rate with limited behavioural support, not the trials' observed rate; the risk ratios are the pooled results. Leaving out the one industry-funded trial in each comparison gave 1.72 (1.23 to 2.39) against nicotine replacement and 1.28 (1.01 to 1.64) against vapes without nicotine, and leaving out high-risk trials gave 1.74 (1.30 to 2.34) and 1.40 (1.09 to 1.81). The review rates the comparison with nicotine replacement high certainty; the editors rate it moderate, because I² is above the 50% mark the review itself calls substantial, its funnel plot is asymmetric (which the authors say could reflect unpublished small trials) and the pool has only 11 trials. How long people kept vaping could not be pooled against nicotine replacement (5 trials, I² 95%): at 6 months or longer more people in the vape group than in the nicotine replacement group were still using their allocated product in 3 trials, and there was no difference in 2. In the five trials that reported product patterns, more people in the vape groups were vaping without smoking (risk ratio 4.40, 1.27 to 15.28; I² 78%; 2,776 people), fewer were using neither cigarettes nor a vape (0.49, 0.26 to 0.91), and possibly fewer were smoking without vaping (0.76, 0.58 to 1.01, an interval that includes no difference; 4 trials; I² 83%); the review's text gives no absolute counts for these, and they are less certain than the quit rates. All participants were adults, follow-up for quitting was 6 months or longer, the trials used regulated nicotine vapes, and the review says longer-term effects are unknown. Of the 80 trials, 8 had tobacco or vaping industry support, and six review authors are authors of included trials (who state they took no part in the inclusion or risk-of-bias decisions for those trials). Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
claims.population: Adults who smoked cigarettes and joined randomised trials of nicotine vapes (80 trials, 29,861 people in the review; 11 trials, 4,114 people against nicotine replacement; 7 trials, 1,918 people against vapes without nicotine); the vape was supplied by the trial in most; Cochrane living review, search to 1 January 2026
claims.exposure: Being given a nicotine vape (cartridge, refillable, pod or disposable devices)
claims.comparator: Nicotine replacement therapy (patch, gum, lozenge or combinations); a vape without nicotine
claims.outcome: Not smoking at 6 months or longer (strictest definition, biochemically confirmed where possible, people lost to follow-up counted as smoking); still using the allocated product, vaping or smoking at that point
claims.magnitude: Cessation at 6+ months. Vs NRT: RR 1.61 (95% CI 1.23–2.12), I² 55%, 11 trials, 4,114 participants; 6 per 100 (assumed) vs 10 per 100 (7–13), about 4 more in 100 (1–7), editors' subtraction; Cochrane high, editors moderate. Vs non-nicotine vape: RR 1.34 (1.05–1.69), I² 0%, 7 trials, 1,918 participants; 6 per 100 (assumed) vs 8 per 100 (6–10), about 2 more in 100 (0–4); moderate. Sensitivity: vs NRT without the industry-funded trial 1.72 (1.23–2.39), without the 2 high-risk trials 1.74 (1.30–2.34); vs non-nicotine without the industry-funded trial 1.28 (1.01–1.64), without the high-risk trial 1.40 (1.09–1.81). Use afterwards vs NRT (not graded): allocated product still in use at 6+ months not pooled (5 trials, I² 95%); vaping without smoking RR 4.40 (1.27–15.28; I² 78%; 2,776); neither vaping nor smoking RR 0.49 (0.26–0.91; I² 31%; 2,776); smoking without vaping RR 0.76 (0.58–1.01; I² 83%; 4 trials; 2,543).
claims.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high, read through a Cochrane living review (random-effects with Hartung-Knapp intervals; AMSTAR 2: high confidence, on the study card). The claim carries the rating of its weakest link. For the comparison with vapes without nicotine the review itself gives moderate (one level for imprecision: fewer than 300 quits; not downgraded for risk of bias, as the one high-risk trial removed gives a larger estimate). For the comparison with nicotine replacement the review gives high, with no downgrade; the editors give moderate, for these reasons: I² is 55%, above the 50% line the review's own Methods call substantial (the review downgraded the adverse-event outcome of the same comparison for I² 72%); the pool's funnel plot is asymmetric, which the Discussion says may reflect publication bias or differences between trials; and with 11 trials the argument the 2018 nicotine replacement authors rely on (so many trials that smaller ones would not change the result) is not available. The editors did not add a second level, because the estimate is unchanged without the industry-funded trial or the high-risk trials and its interval stays well above no difference. The claim is therefore moderate on either route and the senior author may keep the review's high for the comparison with nicotine replacement. Risk of bias, not rated down: 6 of the 11 trials against nicotine replacement were low risk and 2 high; people could not be blinded to vape against patch or gum, but quitting was assessed with biochemical confirmation where possible. Indirectness, not rated down: the claim is limited to adults in trials with trial-supplied, regulated vapes. The use-afterwards figures (product patterns, continued use) are not graded by the review, are heterogeneous (I² 95%, 78%, 83%) and have absolute counts only in figures that were not read; the editors regard them as low certainty and the statement labels them as less certain. One industry-funded trial sits in each pool (Russell 2021, Caponnetto 2013); results hold without them. Status replicated: the comparison with nicotine replacement and the comparison with vapes without nicotine each rest on several trials from different groups and countries; some groups contributed more than one trial and six review authors are authors of included trials. The review is a living review: later updates will change the numbers.

current_lines.q: Do vapes work better than patches or gum for quitting?
current_lines.short: Yes, somewhat. In 11 trials, about 4 more people in 100 quit for 6 months or more with a nicotine vape than with patches or gum.
current_lines.but: In most trials that checked, more people kept using the vape than kept using patches or gum. And effects over years aren't known.
how: A Cochrane review, updated to January 2026, pooled 11 trials with 4,114 adults who smoked; most trials supplied the vape. If 6 in 100 quit with patches or gum, as the review assumes, about 10 in 100 would quit with a nicotine vape.
Against a vape without nicotine, a nicotine vape helped about 2 more in 100 quit, in 7 trials.

What people used afterwards is less certain. In the vape groups, more people were vaping without smoking, and fewer had stopped both smoking and vaping. How long people kept vaping varied too much between trials to combine.
All trials were in adults, with regulated vapes. The results held without the one trial paid for by industry in each comparison, and without the weakest trials.
current_lines.rate: Many trials where chance decided who got a vape. The review rates the evidence strong, but we rate it moderate: results varied between trials, and some small trials that found nothing may be unpublished.

myth_or_fact_items.statement: In trials, nicotine vapes helped more people quit smoking than patches or gum.
myth_or_fact_items.why: In 11 trials, about 4 more people in 100 quit for 6 months or more with a vape than with patches or gum. In most trials that checked, more people kept vaping, and effects over years aren't known.

claims.magnitude: Cessation at 6+ months vs behavioural support only or no support: RR 1.75 (95% CI 1.39–2.20), I² 13%, 11 trials, 7,214 participants; 5 per 100 (assumed) vs 9 per 100 (7–11), about 4 more in 100 (2–6), editors' subtraction; low certainty. Without the industry-funded trial (Xu 2023) 1.53 (1.30–1.79). Advice to use a vape without supplying one vs no advice: RR 1.02 (0.88–1.19), I² 0%, 2 trials, 2,652 participants; unchanged without the high-risk trial; not graded.
claims.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high, read through a Cochrane living review (AMSTAR 2: high confidence, on the study card). Risk of bias, two levels, as the review rates it: the trials could not be blinded and the vape groups received more support than the comparison groups, so some of the difference may come from the extra contact rather than the vape; of the 80 trials in the review 41 were at high risk of bias, and the one trial in this pool with low risk overall gives only a very imprecise result on its own. Inconsistency, not rated down (I² 13%). Indirectness, not rated down: the claim is limited to adults in trials where the vape was supplied. Imprecision, not rated down: 7,214 people and an interval from 1.39 to 2.20. Publication bias, not rated down: the pool's funnel plot is asymmetric (11 trials; the authors say not diagnostic), which the editors do not count as a further level because small unblinded trials that favour the vape are the same worry as the risk-of-bias rating; counting it would give very low. The result holds without the one industry-funded trial (JUUL Labs). The advice-only comparison is not graded by the review; it rests on two trials (one in people who already vaped, one high risk) and its interval (0.88 to 1.19) allows both a modest benefit and a modest harm, so it supports no more than no clear difference. Status replicated: 11 trials by different groups give the same direction with little heterogeneity; the review is a living review and later updates will change the numbers.

current_lines.q: Does vaping actually help people quit smoking?
current_lines.short: It may. In 11 trials, about 4 more people in 100 quit for 6 months or more when given a vape than with counselling alone or nothing.
current_lines.but: People knew they got a vape, and the vape groups got more support too. So part of the gap may come from the extra help.
how: A Cochrane review, updated to January 2026, pooled 11 trials with 7,214 adults who smoked. If 5 in 100 quit with counselling alone or nothing, as the review assumes, about 9 in 100 would quit when given a nicotine vape.
The review rates this low: the trials couldn't hide who got a vape, and the vape groups had more support. The result held without the one trial paid for by a vape company.
Just advising people to vape, without giving them one, made no clear difference, in 2 trials with 2,652 people. All trials were in adults, and longer effects are unknown.
current_lines.rate: Eleven trials where chance decided who got a vape, with results that agree. But people knew what they got, and the vape groups had more support, so the true gain may be smaller.

myth_or_fact_items.statement: Simply advising people who smoke to vape has been shown to help them quit.
myth_or_fact_items.why: In 2 trials, advice to vape without giving a vape made no clear difference. Being given one did better than counselling alone or nothing, but those trials couldn't hide who got a vape.

lines_he_saw_on_13_november.q: Do vapes help people stop smoking, compared with no vape?
lines_he_saw_on_13_november.short: Adults given a nicotine vape stopped smoking more often than those given only counselling or nothing.
lines_he_saw_on_13_november.but: The trials couldn't hide who got the vape, and vape groups often got more support, so the gap may be smaller.
how: After 6 months or more, about 9 in 100 given a vape had stopped, against 5 in 100.
Advising people to vape, without giving them a vape, made no clear difference.
